en: Two o'clock at night. Inside a locomotive cab, the loco pilot is watching the dark track ahead.
visual: REAL: night locomotive cab POV, rain on the windscreen, wiper sweeping; the pilot's hand on the controller.
sound: Cold open: cab hum, rail clatter, no music 2 s

en: Behind that cab, hundreds of families are fast asleep.
visual: REAL: sleeper coach at night, blue night lamp, berths, a child asleep (stock, no faces of real victims).

en: Every time a train crash happens in India, the same fight starts online.
visual: REAL: news archive of a derailment site (credited, short excerpt) cutting to a phone feed scrolling.

en: One side says the government never bothered to install safety technology.
visual: SIM: phone feed, generic posts (no real accounts) reading NO KAVACH? WHY?

en: The other side says Kavach is a magic shield, and crashes are now impossible.
visual: SIM: phone feed, posts reading KAVACH = ZERO ACCIDENTS.

en: Both sides are playing with your feelings. And both are missing the real story.
visual: Both feeds freeze and crack; push through the crack into a dark track bed.

en: So today, let us do this properly. What does Kavach really do?
visual: REAL: Kavach-equipped WAP-7 crossing at speed (Ministry of Railways media).

en: Why can't a train just stop like a car?
visual: REAL: wheel on rail macro, sparks under braking.

en: Why is it working on only a small part of our tracks?
visual: ILLUSTRATION: India rail map, a thin glowing strand among grey lines.

en: And the hardest question... would Kavach have saved Balasore? Would it have saved the Kanchanjunga Express?
visual: REAL: credited news stills of Bahanaga Bazar and Rangapani wreck sites under a forensic magnifier.

en: Hi everyone, welcome to Be Practical with Kishore.
visual: Kishore on camera / channel face card; logo sting.

en: No shouting and no politics. We will use the railway's own documents, simple physics and the official accident reports.
visual: PROOF: RDSO specification cover, CRS abstract cover, PIB release, each under the magnifier.

en: First, the biggest myth. Kavach is not an app, and it is not a software update.
visual: SIM: an app icon labelled KAVACH dissolves into steel hardware.

en: You cannot switch it on across the country overnight.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: a big switch flipped; nothing on the map lights up.

en: Kavach is India's own Automatic Train Protection system. In simple words, it watches the train's speed and the signals ahead.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 1, hardware X-ray): a train on a 3D track; speed and signal readouts float above the cab.

en: If the train goes too fast, or is about to pass a red signal, Kavach first warns the loco pilot.
visual: REAL: Kavach cab display (LP-OCIP) close-up, warning; credited railway media.

en: If the train still does not slow down, Kavach applies the brakes by itself.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: brake command flows from the Kavach box to the brake pipe; speed dial falls.

en: In March twenty twenty two, the Railway Minister rode in a test train in Telangana. Kavach stopped two trains running towards each other on the same line.
visual: REAL: March 2022 Kavach head-on trial footage (Ministry of Railways / PIB release), credited.

en: It looked like magic. But Kavach is not one machine. It is a chain, and it works only when every link is in place.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: four glowing links snap together around a train.

en: Link one is on the track. Small RFID tags are fixed on the concrete sleepers.
visual: REAL: RFID tag on a PSC sleeper (railway media); Engine 1 X-ray marks it.

en: These tags have no battery and no power cable. The reader under the engine wakes them up as it passes.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: under-chassis reader passes over a tag; a radio field ring lights the tag.

en: Each tag tells the train where it is, and on which track.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: tag ID, track ID and location pop as small labels.

en: People say there is one tag every kilometre. That is not the full picture.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: evenly spaced dots on a line, a red cross over them.

en: One kilometre is the longest gap allowed. Near signals, points and stations, there are many more tags.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: dots cluster thickly around a signal and a turnout.

en: On one stretch of about ninety six kilometres near Ahmedabad, the railway fixed two thousand eight hundred and seventy two tags. That is about thirty tags for every kilometre.
visual: BOARD: 2,872 ÷ 96 ≈ 30 worked on the whiteboard, over a map of the stretch.

en: Link two is the station. A Kavach computer at the station reads the signals, the points, and which tracks have a train on them.
visual: REAL: station Kavach equipment room / relay room (railway media).

en: It reads all this from the station's own signalling system, called interlocking. Remember this word. It will matter a lot later.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: interlocking panel lines feed into the Kavach box; the word INTERLOCKING stays lit.

en: Link three is radio. Tall towers along the line carry messages between the station and the engine.
visual: REAL: Kavach lattice tower beside the track (railway media); radio pulses animate to the cab.

en: Kavach's safety radio works in the UHF band. It is not your mobile network, and it is not five G.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: radio band dial; UHF lit, a 5G badge greyed out.

en: Optical fibre cables along the track join the stations together.
visual: REAL: OFC trenching beside railway track (railway media).

en: Link four is inside the engine. A Kavach computer, two RFID readers, speed sensors on the wheels, a screen for the loco pilot, and a link to the brakes.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 1): loco shell peels away layer by layer; each part labels in.

en: Inside that computer, two separate channels check every decision. Both must agree before the train is allowed to move.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: two parallel logic channels, both must light green before a gate opens.

en: It is built to the highest safety level used for railway electronics, called SIL four.
visual: PROOF: SIL-4 band shown on a standards page under the magnifier.

en: Some videos say this means one failure in a billion hours. That is not what it means.
visual: SIM: a viral post reading ONE FAILURE IN A BILLION HOURS, stamped MISLEADING.

en: SIL four is a very strict target for each safety function of the electronics. It is not a promise that no train will ever crash.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: the target applies to one box in the chain, not to the whole railway.

en: And Kavach can only act on the information it gets. Keep that in mind.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: data arrow from interlocking into Kavach glows, then holds.

en: In July twenty twenty four, RDSO, the railway's design body in Lucknow, approved Kavach version four point zero.
visual: PROOF: RDSO / PIB text naming the approval under the magnifier.

en: It brought better location accuracy, better signal information in big yards, fibre links between stations, and a direct link to electronic interlocking.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: four upgrade icons click onto the chain.

en: Now, simple physics. Many people ask me, if the loco pilot sees danger, why can't the train just stop?
visual: REAL: locomotive approaching head-on, low angle.

en: Because a train is not a car. Steel wheels on a steel rail have very little grip.
visual: REAL: car braking on a road vs wheel on rail, split screen.

en: And a train is very heavy, and very long.
visual: REAL: aerial of a long passenger rake on a curve.

en: When the brakes are applied, the air pressure has to change all along the brake pipe, from the engine to the last coach. That takes time.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: air-pressure wave travels down the brake pipe coach by coach.

en: Here is a real number, from an RDSO test certificate.
visual: PROOF: RDSO certificate LH/EO/VAR/78 cover under the magnifier.

en: Twenty four loaded LHB coaches with one WAP seven engine, running at one hundred and thirty kilometres per hour on flat, straight track.
visual: REAL: WAP-7 hauling an LHB rake at speed.

en: With a full service brake, it needed nine hundred and forty metres to stop. Almost one whole kilometre.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 2, braking curve): speed falls along a 940 m track ruler.

en: At that speed, the train covers about thirty six metres every second.
visual: BOARD: 130 ÷ 3.6 ≈ 36 m per second.

en: For Vande Bharat at one hundred and sixty, the railway's own design rule says an emergency stop must take less than one thousand two hundred and fifty metres.
visual: REAL: Vande Bharat at speed; spec page under magnifier.

en: Now think about a loaded goods train. Five thousand tonnes, at seventy five kilometres per hour.
visual: REAL: loaded freight train, long rake of wagons.

en: Goods trains build up brake force slowly. With simple maths and fair guesses, it needs more than nine hundred metres to stop.
visual: BOARD: d = v·t + v²/2a worked live; ≈ 930 m. Label ILLUSTRATIVE MODEL.

en: Put it on a slope going down, one in a hundred, and the same maths gives almost one thousand three hundred metres.
visual: BOARD: gradient term added; ≈ 1,280 m.

en: And if speed goes up from one hundred and thirty to one hundred and sixty, the braking distance does not grow a little. It grows by about half.
visual: BOARD: (160/130)² ≈ 1.5 worked out; curve stretches.

en: That is why speed is the dangerous part.
visual: REAL: speedometer needle in a cab climbing.

en: Now, add winter fog.
visual: REAL: dense winter fog over a north Indian track at dawn.

en: Suppose the loco pilot can see a signal only fifty metres ahead.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 3, fog split): a signal appears out of fog at 50 m.

en: At one hundred and ten kilometres per hour, the train crosses those fifty metres in less than two seconds.
visual: BOARD: 50 ÷ 30.6 ≈ 1.6 s; a stopwatch runs out.

en: Even an alert person needs a second or two just to react. And then the train still needs hundreds of metres to stop.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: reaction gap then stopping distance laid on the track; the stop lands far past the signal.

en: So if safety depends only on human eyes, the maths does not work.
visual: REAL: loco pilot peering into fog (stock, ILLUSTRATIVE FOOTAGE).

en: Kavach changes the question. It does not wait for the loco pilot to see the red signal.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 3): right half of split: cab display shows the signal aspect long before it is visible.

en: It already knows the signal ahead and how far away it is, and shows it on a screen inside the cab.
visual: REAL: Kavach cab display showing target distance and permitted speed.

en: It works out when braking must begin. If the train does not slow down in time, Kavach brakes early, while there is still enough distance.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 2): braking curve drawn ahead of the train; Kavach brake point well before the signal.

en: But Kavach cannot cancel physics. If danger appears closer than the stopping distance, even Kavach cannot stop the train in time.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: obstacle appears inside the curve; red zone.

en: How often do trains pass a red signal by mistake? The Commission of Railway Safety counted two hundred and eight such cases in five years, from April twenty nineteen to March twenty twenty four.
visual: PROOF: CRS abstract page under the magnifier; counter rolls to 208.

en: Twelve of them ended in a collision.
visual: Counter splits: 12 turns red.

en: This is exactly the kind of human mistake Kavach is built to catch.
visual: REAL: red signal at night, train slowing.

en: So if Kavach is this useful, why is it not on every track today?
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 4, rollout funnel): national map, grey.

en: Did the government refuse to spend money? Let us look at the numbers.
visual: PROOF: PIB release page under magnifier.

en: First, the size of the job. Indian Railways has about sixty nine thousand route kilometres.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: map lines draw in across India.

en: That counts each route once. Count every parallel line, and the running track is more than one lakh eleven thousand kilometres.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: single lines split into double and quadruple lines.

en: And there are about sixteen thousand diesel and electric engines.
visual: REAL: loco shed with rows of engines.

en: Now, the progress. By the end of July twenty twenty six, the newest Kavach version was working on two thousand six hundred and thirty three route kilometres.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 4): two corridors glow on the map.

en: That is on parts of the Delhi Mumbai and Delhi Howrah routes, two of the busiest in the country.
visual: Map labels: 1,423 km Delhi–Mumbai group, 1,210 km Delhi–Howrah group.

en: An older version also runs on about one thousand four hundred and sixty five kilometres in South Central Railway. Parts of it are now being upgraded.
visual: Map: SCR section glows in a second colour; upgrade arrow on Malkajgiri–Kamareddi.

en: So even if you count both, Kavach is working on well under a tenth of the network.
And here is the trap in many news posts. Different numbers mean different things.
visual: SIM: three headlines with big numbers, each blurred except the number.

en: Track where equipment is fitted, seven thousand seven hundred and twenty six kilometres.
visual: Funnel tier 2.

en: Engines fitted with Kavach, six thousand two hundred and ninety.
visual: REAL: loco Kavach cabinet being fitted in a shed.

en: Track where work has started, twenty one thousand seven hundred and ninety four kilometres.
visual: Funnel tier 3 (widest).

en: Fitted is not the same as working. And work started is not the same as protected.
visual: Funnel narrows to the thin working stream.

en: So, is money the problem? The yearly Kavach budget went from about one thousand one hundred crore rupees in twenty twenty four twenty five, to about one thousand six hundred and seventy crore the next year.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: two budget bars rise.

en: By June twenty twenty six, about three thousand eight hundred and seventy five crore rupees had been spent on Kavach in total.
visual: Bar fills to cumulative.

en: Now some rough maths. The government's estimate is about fifty lakh rupees per kilometre for the track side, and about eighty lakh rupees per engine.
visual: BOARD: ₹50 lakh/km · ₹80 lakh/loco written up.

en: Fifty lakh per kilometre, for about sixty nine thousand kilometres, comes to nearly thirty five thousand crore rupees.
Eighty lakh per engine, for sixteen thousand engines, adds about twelve thousand eight hundred crore more.
This is rough maths, not an official bill. But it shows you the size of the job.
visual: BOARD: ROUGH MATHS boxed.

en: Still, the hardest part is not buying boxes. It is making them all work together.
visual: REAL: signalling technicians at a relay rack.

en: Every station's signalling data must be entered and checked. Every type of engine must be wired to its own brakes.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (flowchart): survey → data → loco fitment.

en: Radio must cover every curve and every yard. Then everything is tested together, fixed, and tested again, before a single kilometre is called working.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (flowchart): integrated trials loop back on failure; only then COMMISSIONED.

en: So the slowest step sets the speed of the whole rollout.
visual: Flowchart bottleneck box pulses.

en: Suppliers matter too. For years, three Indian companies supplied Kavach, Medha, HBL and Kernex.
visual: PROOF: SCR Kavach overview listing the three firms.

en: New companies are trying to join. One of them, Quadrant Future Tek, got permission for passenger trials in May twenty twenty six. That is a step, not final approval.
visual: PROOF: company stock-exchange filing under magnifier.

en: Now, the two most painful questions.
visual: Black frame, slow fade up on twisted coaches (credited archive).

en: Would Kavach have stopped Balasore? And would it have saved the Kanchanjunga Express?
visual: Split screen: Balasore and Rangapani archive stills.

en: Case one. Bahanaga Bazar station, near Balasore in Odisha. June two, twenty twenty three.
visual: REAL: credited archive of the Bahanaga Bazar site; map pin.

en: The Coromandel Express was coming in at about one hundred and twenty eight kilometres per hour.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 5, logic gate): station layout, train arrow on the up main line.

en: The signal showed green, for the main line.
visual: Engine 5: home signal turns green.

en: But the crossover ahead was set towards the loop line, where a goods train was standing.
visual: Engine 5: crossover 17A/B swings to the loop; parked goods train highlighted. ILLUSTRATION.

en: The official inquiry found lapses in signalling circuit work done at the station.
visual: PROOF: CRS abstract finding under magnifier.

en: Close to three hundred people lost their lives.
visual: Slow push on candles / memorial still (credited); no victims shown.

en: So, would Kavach have stopped it?
visual: Engine 5: a Kavach box appears on the loco; question mark avoided, the box pulses.
sound: Total silence 1.5 s after this line

en: Here is the honest answer. Nobody can say yes or no for sure.
visual: Kishore / dark track bed.

en: Remember, Kavach reads the signals and the points from the station's interlocking.
visual: Engine 5: interlocking feed lights up into Kavach.

en: At Balasore, the signalling system itself was showing a false green. If Kavach was given the same wrong information, it could also believe the line was clear.
visual: Engine 5: the false green travels down the wire into Kavach, which shows green too. ILLUSTRATION.

en: A safety computer cannot correct wrong information that it trusts.
visual: Engine 5: both channels agree on the wrong input; gate opens.

en: Kavach does have some extra checks of its own, like knowing from the tags which track the train is really on. Whether those checks would have acted in time there, no public study has shown.
visual: Engine 5: tag reads appear on the loop line, dotted, uncertain.

en: So people who say Kavach would surely have saved Balasore, and people who say it surely could not, are both going beyond the evidence.
visual: The two viral posts from the hook return, both stamped BEYOND THE EVIDENCE.

en: Case two. Between Rangapani and Chatterhat, near New Jalpaiguri in north Bengal. June seventeen, twenty twenty four.
visual: REAL: credited archive of the Rangapani site; map pin.

en: The automatic signals on this stretch had failed.
visual: ILLUSTRATION (Engine 6): a row of automatic signals goes dark.

en: When that happens, trains move on a paper authority, at a slow and careful speed.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: a generic paper authority slides in (no copy of a real form).

en: The inquiry found the goods train was given the wrong form, T A nine one two, instead of T D nine one two.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: two distinct labels T/A 912 and T/D 912; the wrong one highlighted.

en: No caution order was given. Walkie talkies were missing. And training was not good enough.
visual: Three items tick red: caution order, walkie-talkie, training.

en: The goods train reached seventy eight kilometres per hour, and hit the Kanchanjunga Express from behind at about forty.
visual: Engine 6: freight speed trace climbs to 78, collision marked at ~40.

en: There was no working Kavach on that section.
visual: Engine 6: map overlay, no Kavach line here.

en: Here, Kavach could have made a real difference.
visual: Engine 6 rewinds; a Kavach box appears on both locos. SIMULATION.

en: If both trains were fitted and the section was working, Kavach could have enforced the allowed movement and a slow speed past the failed signals.
visual: Engine 6: freight speed held low; braking curve stops it short. SIMULATION.

en: Some videos say Kavach would lock the speed at exactly fifteen kilometres per hour, every time. That depends on the mode and the rules set. The documents do not promise it so simply.
visual: SIM: viral claim card stamped DEPENDS ON MODE.

en: And this was not just one loco pilot's mistake. The inquiry found failures in the paperwork, the communication and the training.
visual: Engine 6: the three red ticks return around the station building.

en: So, two crashes, two different failures. At Balasore, the signalling information itself was wrong. At Kanchanjunga, the backup rules for failed signals broke down.
visual: Side-by-side comparison: two columns, two icons.

en: Kavach is strongest against the second kind. Against the first, the fix has to start in the signalling room.
visual: REAL: technician testing a relay rack.

en: So, what is the practical truth?
visual: REAL: dawn, a train crossing a bridge.

en: Kavach is not magic. And it is not useless.
visual: The two myths from the hook fade out.

en: It is a strong extra layer. It brakes early when a human makes a speed or signal mistake.
visual: Engine 2 curve, Kavach brake point.

en: But it needs four things to work. A fitted engine, a working track section, correct signalling data, and enough distance to stop.
visual: The four links from Act 1 relight one by one.

en: Next time you see a viral post about Kavach, ask three simple questions.
visual: REAL: hand scrolling a phone on a station platform.

en: One. Is this number about fitted equipment, or about Kavach that is actually working?
visual: Card 1 in a lower corner.

en: Two. Which date is this number from?
visual: Card 2.

en: Three. Was the problem a human mistake, or wrong information from the signalling system?
visual: Card 3.

en: Real safety is not built on slogans. It is built on careful, boring engineering, done right every single day.
visual: REAL: track maintenance gang at work at sunrise; relay room.

en: If someone you love travels by train, share this video with them. Be smart, be informed, and always... be practical.
visual: Logo bug, end card.
